title: Prices and Jobs: The CPI and Unemployment
bigQuestion: How do we know whether prices are really rising and whether people can really find work, and what do those two numbers miss?

story.title: Grandpa's Dollar Sixty
story.kicker: A grandfather remembers his first paycheck, and his granddaughter sets out to learn whether $1.60 an hour was a good wage.
paragraphs: Maya sat at her grandfather's kitchen table in Joliet with a notebook, interviewing him for a school project. He told her about his first job, in 1968, stocking shelves at a grocery store after school. It paid $1.60 an hour, the federal minimum wage that year. Maya laughed. She makes $15 an hour at a sandwich shop, the Illinois minimum wage. You made about a tenth of what I make, she said.

Her grandfather was not bothered. He remembered filling his car with gas for well under half a dollar a gallon and seeing a movie for a dollar or two. A hamburger at the drive-in cost less than a quarter, as he recalled it. His paycheck was small, he said, but so was everything else. Maya started to suspect that comparing his dollars with hers was like comparing two different currencies.

So she looked up the Consumer Price Index, the number the Bureau of Labor Statistics uses to track prices. It averaged about 35 in 1968 and about 313 in 2024. Prices had risen almost nine times. Multiply $1.60 by about 8.9 and you get roughly $14 in 2024 dollars. Her grandfather's wage bought close to what her $15 buys. It bought about twice what today's federal minimum of $7.25 buys.

Then Maya asked a second question: was it easy to find that job? Her grandfather said help-wanted signs were everywhere in 1968. He was right; the national unemployment rate that year was under 4%. Maya's father had a different story. He finished college in 2009, when unemployment was near 10%, and spent eight months sending out applications before anyone called him back.

Maya's project had turned into the two questions this chapter answers. How do we measure what money is worth from year to year? And how do we count the people who want work and cannot find it? The government reports both numbers every month, and millions of decisions, from raises to interest rates, depend on them.
story.think: Maya's $15 and her grandfather's $1.60 were both minimum wages. Besides prices, what else would you want to know to decide which of them had the better deal?

lessons.title: Building a Price Index
lessons.mainIdea: The CPI tracks the cost of a fixed market basket of goods and services, compared with a base year set equal to 100.
reading: Suppose a student named Jordan buys the same things every month: 10 gallons of gas, 4 pizzas and 2 movie tickets. In the base year, gas is $3 a gallon, pizza $10 and a ticket $15. The basket costs 10 x $3 + 4 x $10 + 2 x $15 = $30 + $40 + $30 = $100. A year later gas is $3.60, pizza $10.50 and a ticket $16. The same basket now costs $36 + $42 + $32 = $110. Jordan buys exactly the same things and pays $10 more.

A *market basket* is a fixed list of goods and services in fixed amounts, chosen to stand for what a typical buyer purchases. A *price index* turns the basket's cost into one simple number. The rule: index = cost of the basket this year divided by its cost in the *base year*, times 100. For Jordan, 110 divided by 100, times 100 = 110. The base year always equals 100, so an index of 110 means prices are 10% above the base year.

The *Consumer Price Index*, or CPI, uses the same method for the whole country. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, part of the U.S. Department of Labor, collects tens of thousands of prices each month in cities across the country. It prices food, rent, gas, clothing, doctor visits, car insurance and much more. Each item is weighted by the share of household budgets spent on it. So a rise in rent moves the index far more than a rise in the price of salt. The BLS publishes the CPI every month.

The official CPI uses the years 1982 to 1984 as its base, set to 100. In 2024 the index stood a little above 310. That means a basket that cost $100 in the early 1980s cost a little over $310 in 2024. A common mistake is to read an index number as a price. A CPI of 310 does not mean anything costs $310. It means prices are about 3.1 times their base-period level.

words.d: a fixed list of goods and services in fixed amounts that stands for what a typical buyer purchases
a number comparing the cost of a basket in one year with its cost in a base year, where the base year equals 100
the year (or years) whose prices a price index is compared against; the index equals 100 then
the CPI; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly measure of the prices city households pay for a market basket

look.title: One Basket, Four Years (example)
look.cite: Invented basket costs, used only to practice building an index
look.prompt: Compute the price index for each year, with Year 1 as the base. By what percent did prices rise from Year 1 to Year 4?

check.q: A basket costs $80 in the base year and $92 this year. The price index this year is:
check.why: Index = 92 / 80 x 100 = 115. Prices are 15% above the base year.

check.q: Which agency publishes the Consumer Price Index?
choices: The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
check.why: The BLS, in the Department of Labor, collects prices and publishes the CPI each month. The BEA publishes GDP.

check.q: The CPI is 250. What does that tell you?
choices: Prices are 250% lower than in the base period
The basket costs 2.5 times what it cost in the base period
check.why: An index compares with a base of 100. At 250, the basket costs 250 / 100 = 2.5 times its base-period cost.

lessons.title: The Inflation Rate
lessons.mainIdea: The inflation rate is the percent change in the price index from one period to the next, not the difference in index points.
reading: Jordan's basket index went from 100 to 110 in one year. The *inflation rate* is the percent change in the price level: (110 - 100) divided by 100, times 100 = 10%. Now go one more year. The index rises from 110 to 121. The change is 11 points, but the inflation rate is 11 divided by 110, times 100 = 10%, not 11%. Always divide the change by the starting index. Subtracting index points works only when the starting index is exactly 100.

Real figures work the same way. If the CPI was 300 last June and 312 this June, inflation over those twelve months was 12 divided by 300, times 100 = 4%. News reports usually give this 12-month rate. They also report *core inflation*, which leaves out food and energy. Those two prices jump around with weather, wars and oil supplies. Leaving them out shows the steadier trend underneath.

*Inflation* is a rise in the general level of prices, not a rise in one price. Suppose avocados jump after a bad harvest while most other prices hold still. That is a change in a *relative price*, not inflation. Inflation means the whole basket costs more, so each dollar buys less. The Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over time. It treats a small, steady rate as healthier than either high inflation or falling prices.

U.S. inflation has swung widely. It reached about 13.5% for the year 1980, then fell during the 1980s. From the mid-1990s through 2020 it mostly stayed between about 1% and 4%. It jumped again in 2021 and 2022, and the 12-month rate peaked near 9% in mid-2022 before coming down. Knowing these rough figures helps you judge whether a year's number is ordinary or alarming.

words.d: a rise in the general level of prices, so each dollar buys less
the percent change in a price index over a period, usually a year
inflation measured without food and energy prices, which swing a lot from month to month
the price of one good compared with other goods; one price rising alone is not inflation

look.title: U.S. Inflation, Selected Years
look.cite: Rounded yearly-average changes in the CPI for all urban consumers, Bureau of Labor Statistics
look.prompt: Which years were close to the Fed's 2% goal? In which year did a dollar lose the most buying power, and about how much?

check.q: The CPI rises from 200 to 210. The inflation rate is:
check.why: (210 - 200) / 200 x 100 = 5%. The 10-point rise is not 10% because the starting index is 200, not 100.

check.q: The CPI goes from 120 to 126. The inflation rate is:
check.why: 6 / 120 x 100 = 5%. Dividing by the ending index, 126, gives the wrong 4.8%.

check.q: Beef prices rise 20% after a drought while most other prices stay flat. This is best described as:
check.why: Inflation is a rise in the general price level. One good rising alone is a change in relative prices.

lessons.title: Where the CPI Misses
lessons.mainIdea: Because the basket is fixed and quality keeps changing, the CPI can overstate the true rise in living costs, and no family's own inflation matches it exactly.
reading: Suppose beef jumps from $6 to $9 a pound while chicken stays at $4. Many families switch from beef to chicken. A fixed basket still assumes they buy the old amount of beef. So it shows their costs rising more than they really did. This is *substitution bias*. The BLS reduces it by updating the basket's weights regularly and by allowing for some switching within categories, such as from one kind of apple to another. It cannot remove the problem completely.

Quality is the second problem. A new phone may cost $800, the same as a phone five years ago, but it has a better camera, more storage and a faster chip. If the price is the same and the phone is better, the true price of what you get has fallen. The BLS makes a *quality adjustment* for some goods, but valuing an improvement is hard. New goods raise a third problem. When a new kind of product appears, it takes time to enter the basket, so its arrival does not register as a gain.

Economists have long argued that together these effects make the CPI overstate the true rise in the *cost of living*, by a fraction of a percentage point a year. That matters because the CPI adjusts real payments. Social Security benefits rise each year with a version of the CPI. Federal income tax brackets are adjusted with a version of it too. A CPI that runs a little high raises those payments a little faster than living costs.

Finally, the CPI is an average, and no family is average. A renter in Chicago whose rent jumps 8% faces higher inflation than a homeowner with a paid-off house. A long commute makes gas prices matter more. An older person spends more on health care. When your own costs rise faster or slower than the CPI, the index is not wrong. Your basket is simply different from the national one.

words.d: the tendency of a fixed basket to overstate rising costs because people switch away from goods whose prices jump
a change the BLS makes to a price to account for a product getting better or worse
the amount of money needed to buy the goods and services a household uses

look.title: The Phone That Cost the Same
look.text: In Year 1 a phone costs $600 and holds 64 gigabytes. In Year 3 a phone costs $600 and holds 256 gigabytes, with a much better camera and a battery that lasts twice as long. The person building the price index has to decide what happened to the price of phones.
look.prompt: Did the price of a phone rise, fall or stay the same? Explain why counting it as unchanged would make the CPI overstate inflation.

check.q: Beef prices double while chicken prices stay flat, and families switch to chicken. A fixed basket will:
choices: Understate the rise in their costs
Overstate the rise in their costs
check.why: The fixed basket assumes families still buy the old amount of beef, so it shows costs rising more than they did. This is substitution bias.

check.q: A laptop's price stays at $900 but it becomes twice as fast. With no quality adjustment, the CPI would:
choices: Remove the laptop from the basket
Count the laptop as a transfer payment
Miss a real fall in the price per unit of quality
check.why: The buyer gets more for the same $900, so the true price fell. A CPI that records no change misses that fall.

check.q: Which government payment rises each year with a version of the CPI?
choices: Grain prices at the Chicago Board of Trade
check.why: Social Security has a yearly cost-of-living adjustment tied to a CPI. The federal minimum wage changes only when Congress passes a law.

lessons.title: Purchasing Power and Real Wages
lessons.mainIdea: To compare dollars from different years, adjust with the CPI; a real wage rises only when pay grows faster than prices.
reading: *Purchasing power* is how much a dollar can buy. When prices rise 25%, a dollar buys only about four-fifths of what it used to, because 1 divided by 1.25 = 0.80. Inflation does not take dollars out of your wallet. It shrinks what each dollar will get you. That is why comparing a wage from 1968 with a wage today is like comparing two different currencies. You have to convert first.

The conversion uses the CPI: value in today's dollars = old amount x (CPI today divided by CPI then). The CPI averaged about 35 in 1968 and about 313 in 2024. So prices rose about 313 divided by 35, or roughly 8.9 times. Grandpa's $1.60 an hour x 8.9 = about $14.24 in 2024 dollars. The federal minimum wage of $7.25, unchanged since 2009, buys only about half of what the 1968 minimum bought. Illinois set its own minimum at $15 an hour in 2025.

A *nominal wage* is pay in the dollars of the day. A *real wage* is pay adjusted for prices, which shows what the pay can buy. Suppose Ana's wage rises from $15.00 to $15.60 an hour, a 4% raise, while prices rise 6%. Her nominal wage went up, but her real wage fell about 2%. In last year's dollars, $15.60 divided by 1.06 is about $14.72, less than the $15.00 she earned before. The quick rule: real wage growth is about nominal wage growth minus inflation.

The common mistake is to call any raise a gain. A raise smaller than inflation is a pay cut in what matters: goods and services. That is why many workers push for a *cost-of-living adjustment*, a raise tied to the CPI. It is also why economists compare wages over time only in real terms. In 2021 and 2022 many workers got their biggest raises in years. Yet for much of that time prices rose even faster, so real wages fell for many of them.

words.d: the amount of goods and services a sum of money can buy
pay measured in the dollars of the day, not adjusted for prices
pay adjusted for inflation, which shows what the pay can actually buy
an automatic raise in pay or benefits tied to the rise in a price index such as the CPI

look.title: Adjusting Grandpa's Wage
look.cite: CPI values rounded from Bureau of Labor Statistics data; $1.60 was the federal minimum wage in 1968
look.prompt: Divide the 2024 CPI by the 1968 CPI, then multiply by the wage. What is $1.60 worth in 2024 dollars? How does it compare with $7.25 and with $15?

check.q: Your wage rises 3% and prices rise 5%. Your real wage:
check.why: Real wage growth is about nominal growth minus inflation: 3 - 5 = -2%. Your pay buys less than before.

check.q: A movie ticket cost $2 when the CPI was 50. The CPI is now 300. In today's dollars, that ticket cost:
check.why: $2 x (300 / 50) = $2 x 6 = $12. Prices are six times higher, so the old $2 equals $12 today.

check.q: After all prices double, a $100 bill buys about as much as how many dollars bought before?
check.why: When prices double, each dollar buys half as much: 100 / 2 = $50 of old buying power.

lessons.title: Winners and Losers From Inflation
lessons.mainIdea: Unexpected inflation moves buying power from lenders to borrowers and from people on fixed incomes to people whose pay keeps up.
reading: Suppose you lend a friend $1,000 for one year at 5% interest. You expect to get back $1,050. If prices rise 2% that year, your gain in buying power is about 3%. If prices unexpectedly rise 7%, the $1,050 you get back buys less than the $1,000 did when you lent it. The *nominal interest rate* was 5%. The *real interest rate*, the nominal rate minus inflation, was about 5 - 7 = -2%. The borrower won and the lender lost.

That is the core pattern: unexpected inflation helps people who owe fixed dollar amounts and hurts people who are owed them. A family with a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage repays with dollars that are worth less each year, which helps them. The bank that made the loan loses. Savers lose too. Put $10,000 in an account paying 1% while inflation runs 4%. It earns $100 in interest while prices rise about $400 worth, a real loss of about $300.

People on a *fixed income* also lose, such as a retiree whose pension pays the same $2,000 a month every year. Some incomes are protected. Social Security has a yearly cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI, and some union contracts include one. Workers whose raises keep pace with prices come out about even. The key word is unexpected. If everyone expects 7% inflation, lenders charge higher rates in advance, and the transfer mostly disappears.

Inflation also has costs that fall on everyone. Stores must reprint prices and menus, called *menu costs*. People spend time and effort guarding their cash. Businesses and families find it harder to plan when they cannot tell what a dollar will buy next year. High and changeable inflation makes long-term contracts risky. That is one reason central banks aim for low, steady inflation.

words.d: the interest rate stated on a loan or account, not adjusted for inflation
the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate; the gain in buying power a lender actually gets
income that stays the same number of dollars each year, such as some pensions
the costs businesses pay to change prices, such as reprinting menus and price tags

look.title: Three People, One Surprise
look.text: Inflation was expected to be 2% but turns out to be 6%. Keisha owes $200,000 on a fixed-rate mortgage at 4%. Mr. Patel, retired, lives on a pension of $2,500 a month that never changes. Luis is a nurse whose union contract raises his pay each year by the CPI inflation rate.
look.prompt: Who gains, who loses and who breaks about even? Name the rule that explains each case.

check.q: A bank lends at 6% and inflation turns out to be 8%. The real interest rate is about:
check.why: Real rate = nominal rate - inflation = 6 - 8 = -2%. The bank is repaid in dollars that buy less than the ones it lent.

check.q: Unexpectedly high inflation usually helps which group?
check.why: Borrowers repay a fixed number of dollars, and those dollars are worth less. The other three are owed or hold fixed dollars.

check.q: Why does fully expected inflation shift little buying power from lenders to borrowers?
choices: Because expected inflation is always zero
Because lenders build the expected inflation into the interest rate
check.why: If lenders expect 7% inflation, they raise the nominal rate to cover it, so the real rate they earn is protected.

lessons.title: Deflation and Runaway Inflation
lessons.mainIdea: Falling prices sound good but can deepen a slump, and very rapid inflation, usually caused by printing money, can wreck an economy.
reading: *Deflation* is a fall in the general price level, a negative inflation rate. At first it sounds like a gift: the same $100 buys more. But look at a family that owes $100,000 on a house. If prices and wages both fall 10%, the family's income drops from, say, $50,000 to $45,000, while the debt stays at $100,000. The debt is now harder to carry. Across a whole economy, falling prices make debts heavier, and more people fall behind on loans.

Deflation also changes behavior. If you expect a $1,000 refrigerator to cost $950 next year, you may wait. When millions of people wait, stores sell less, cut jobs and cut prices again. Economists call this a deflationary spiral. It happened in the Great Depression, when U.S. consumer prices fell by roughly a quarter between 1929 and 1933. Do not confuse deflation with *disinflation*, which means inflation is slowing, say from 6% to 3%. Prices are still rising, only more slowly.

At the other extreme is *hyperinflation*, inflation so fast that prices climb by huge amounts each month or even each day. Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in the late 2000s are standard examples. In both cases the government paid its bills by printing money far faster than the economy grew. Workers rushed to spend their pay before it lost value. People turned to barter or foreign currency, and saving became pointless.

These two dangers help explain the Federal Reserve's 2% target. A small positive rate leaves some room above zero, so a slump is less likely to tip into deflation. It is also low enough that people can plan without constantly thinking about prices. The lesson from both extremes is the same. A stable, predictable price level is part of what lets a market economy work.

words.d: a fall in the general level of prices; a negative inflation rate
a slowdown in the inflation rate; prices still rise, but more slowly
extremely rapid inflation, usually caused by a government printing money to pay its bills
a cycle in which falling prices lead people to delay buying, which cuts sales, jobs and prices further

look.title: Buy the Car Now or Wait?
look.text: Prices in a country have fallen 3% a year for four years. You need a car that costs $20,000 today, and you expect it to cost about $19,400 next year. Your pay has been cut twice, and you still owe $8,000 on a student loan.
look.prompt: Would you buy now or wait? What happens to the whole economy if everyone makes the same choice? What is happening to the real burden of your loan?

check.q: Inflation falls from 5% to 2%. This is:
check.why: Prices are still rising, just more slowly. That is disinflation. Deflation would mean prices actually fall.

check.q: During deflation, a family with a fixed $50,000 debt finds that:
choices: The debt is harder to repay, because incomes and prices fall while the debt does not
The debt is easier to repay
check.why: The dollar amount owed stays the same while wages fall, so each payment takes a bigger share of income.

check.q: The most common cause of hyperinflation is:
choices: A drought that raises food prices
A government printing money far faster than output grows
A rise in the minimum wage
check.why: Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in the 2000s both printed money to pay government bills, so money lost value very fast.

lessons.title: Who Is in the Labor Force
lessons.mainIdea: Each month the government sorts adults into employed, unemployed and not in the labor force; only people without work who are looking count as unemployed.
reading: Picture four people on one block in Aurora. Dana works 20 hours a week at a hardware store. Marcus lost his warehouse job and has sent out ten applications this month. Priya is a full-time college student who is not looking for work. Mr. Lopez retired last year. Only Marcus is unemployed in the official sense. Dana has a job, even though it is part-time. Priya and Mr. Lopez have no job, but they are not looking, so they are not in the labor force at all.

The rules come from the *Current Population Survey*, which the Census Bureau conducts for the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Each month it interviews about 60,000 households. People 16 and older, not in the military or in places such as prisons, are sorted into three groups. *Employed*: did any work for pay in the survey week, or had a job but were out sick or on vacation. *Unemployed*: had no job, were available to work, and actively looked in the past four weeks, or were waiting to be called back from a layoff.

The *labor force* is the employed plus the unemployed: everyone who has a job or is looking for one. Try the numbers for a town with 10,000 adults. If 6,000 are employed and 400 are unemployed, the labor force is 6,000 + 400 = 6,400. The other 3,600 are *not in the labor force*. They include students, retirees, stay-at-home parents, people too ill to work, and people who want a job but have stopped looking.

A common mistake is to think unemployed means anyone without a job. By that count Priya, Mr. Lopez and a stay-at-home father would all be unemployed, and the number would be huge and meaningless. The official definition asks two questions. Do you have a job? If not, are you looking? The survey counts actions, such as sending applications or contacting employers. Wishing for work is not enough.

words.d: all people 16 and older who are employed or unemployed; everyone working or looking for work
did any work for pay in the survey week, or had a job but was temporarily away from it
had no job, was available to work, and actively looked for work in the past four weeks
adults who neither have a job nor are looking, such as students, retirees and stay-at-home parents
the monthly survey of about 60,000 households that the government uses to measure employment and unemployment

look.title: Sort the Neighbors
look.text: Six people in Rockford: a high school junior who works 10 hours a week at a grocery store; a laid-off machinist who interviewed for two jobs this month; a mother caring for a newborn who plans to go back to work next year; a retired teacher, age 70; a college graduate who applied for jobs until six weeks ago and then gave up; a nurse home sick this week from her full-time job.
look.prompt: Place each person in employed, unemployed or not in the labor force. Which placement might surprise a reader, and why?

check.q: A 17-year-old works 6 hours a week for pay at a pet store. Officially, she is:
choices: Not in the labor force, because she is a student
Not counted, because she is under 18
check.why: Anyone 16 or older who did any work for pay in the survey week counts as employed, even part-time.

check.q: Which person is counted as unemployed?
choices: A retiree who does not want a job
A student who is not looking for work
A worker who stopped looking three months ago
A laid-off worker who applied for jobs last week
check.why: Unemployed means no job, available, and actively looking in the past four weeks. Only the laid-off worker meets all three.

check.q: A town has 8,000 employed, 500 unemployed and 3,500 adults not in the labor force. The labor force is:
check.why: Labor force = employed + unemployed = 8,000 + 500 = 8,500. People not in the labor force are left out.

lessons.title: The Unemployment Rate
lessons.mainIdea: The unemployment rate is the number unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100, not divided by the whole adult population.
reading: Use the town from the last lesson: 6,000 employed, 400 unemployed, a labor force of 6,400. The *unemployment rate* = unemployed divided by labor force, times 100 = 400 divided by 6,400, times 100 = 6.25%. About 6 of every 100 people who want work and are looking cannot find it. The most common mistake is dividing by all 10,000 adults, which gives 4%. That understates the problem, because it treats retirees and students who are not looking as if they had jobs.

The BLS reports the national rate early each month, usually on the first Friday, in a release called the Employment Situation. The survey is a sample, so small moves of 0.1 or 0.2 points may be noise. Illinois and its counties and cities have their own rates, estimated each month by the Illinois Department of Employment Security working with the BLS. Local rates can differ a lot from the national one. A factory closing hits one county much harder than the whole country.

History gives a sense of scale. Unemployment reached about 25% in 1933, the worst of the Great Depression. It rose to nearly 11% in late 1982, and to about 10% in late 2009 after the financial crisis. In April 2020, as businesses shut down in the pandemic, it jumped to 14.7% in a single month. Then it fell faster than almost anyone expected. In strong years such as 2019 and 2023 the rate stayed below 4%.

Always check what a change is measuring. Suppose the number unemployed rises from 400 to 480 while the labor force stays at 6,400. The rate goes from 6.25% to 7.5%. That is a rise of 1.25 *percentage points*, but a 20% increase in the number of unemployed people. News stories sometimes mix those up. A percentage point is the difference between two rates. A percent change compares a new number with the old one.

words.d: the number unemployed divided by the labor force, times 100
the plain difference between two percentages; going from 4% to 5% is a rise of 1 percentage point
a smaller group surveyed to estimate facts about a whole population

look.title: U.S. Unemployment, Selected Moments
look.cite: Rounded from Bureau of Labor Statistics data; the 1933 figure is a later estimate
look.prompt: Which moment was the worst? About how many times higher was the rate in April 2020 than in 2023? What was happening in the economy at the two moments near 10%?

check.q: A city has 45,000 people employed and 5,000 unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
check.why: Labor force = 45,000 + 5,000 = 50,000. Rate = 5,000 / 50,000 x 100 = 10%. Dividing by the employed gives the wrong 11.1%.

check.q: A country has 200 million adults, a labor force of 150 million and 9 million unemployed. The unemployment rate is:
check.why: 9 / 150 x 100 = 6%. Dividing by all 200 million adults gives the wrong 4.5%.

check.q: The unemployment rate rises from 4% to 5%. Which statement is correct?
choices: It rose 1 percentage point, a 25% increase in the rate
check.why: 5 - 4 = 1 percentage point. As a percent change, 1 / 4 x 100 = 25%.

lessons.title: Discouraged Workers and Participation
lessons.mainIdea: The participation rate shows what share of adults are working or looking, and discouraged workers can make unemployment look lower than it feels.
reading: Back in the town of 10,000 adults, 6,400 are in the labor force. The *labor force participation rate* = labor force divided by adult population, times 100 = 6,400 divided by 10,000, times 100 = 64%. It answers a different question from the unemployment rate: how many adults are taking part in the job market at all? In the United States the participation rate peaked a little above 67% around 2000. In recent years it has been near 62% to 63%.

Now suppose 100 of the 400 unemployed people give up. They have looked for months and believe no jobs are out there, so they stop searching. They are now *discouraged workers*, and they leave the labor force. The number unemployed falls to 300 and the labor force to 6,300. The unemployment rate drops to 300 divided by 6,300, times 100 = about 4.8%. Nobody found a job, yet the headline rate fell from 6.25% to 4.8%. The participation rate fell to 63%, and that is the clue.

The unemployment rate also misses *underemployment*. A worker who wants full-time hours but can find only 15 hours a week counts as employed. So does a college graduate in a job that needs no degree. The BLS publishes a broader measure, called U-6. It adds discouraged workers, others loosely attached to the job market, and people working part-time who want full-time work. U-6 always runs well above the official rate.

Why has participation fallen since 2000? The biggest single reason is age. The large baby boom generation has been retiring, and retirees leave the labor force. Young people staying in school longer also play a part. Economists debate how much of the rest reflects weak job prospects, health problems or other causes. The lesson for reading the news: look at unemployment and participation together, because either one alone can mislead.

words.d: the labor force divided by the adult population, times 100; the share of adults working or looking
people who want a job but have stopped looking because they believe none is available; they are not counted as unemployed
working fewer hours than wanted, or in a job that does not use one's skills

look.title: Good News or Bad?
look.text: A headline says: Unemployment falls from 7.0% to 6.6%. Deep in the report, the number of employed people did not change at all. The labor force shrank by 400,000 as people stopped looking for work.
look.prompt: Is the drop in unemployment good news? Explain what happened using the terms discouraged workers and participation rate.

check.q: A state has 5 million adults, and 3.2 million are in the labor force. The participation rate is:
check.why: 3.2 / 5 x 100 = 64%. The participation rate divides the labor force by the adult population.

check.q: When discouraged workers stop looking, the official unemployment rate:
choices: Rises, because more people are jobless
Falls, even though no one found a job
Stays the same, because they are still counted
check.why: They leave both the unemployed count and the labor force, so the rate falls without anyone getting hired.

check.q: A worker wants 40 hours a week but can get only 12. Officially, the worker is counted as:
check.why: Any paid work in the survey week counts as employed. The shortfall in hours is underemployment, which the headline rate misses.

lessons.title: Between Jobs and Out of Season
lessons.mainIdea: Some unemployment is normal: people between jobs (frictional) and people whose work follows the calendar (seasonal).
reading: Tanya finishes a nursing degree at Northern Illinois University in May. She applies to four hospitals and starts her first job in August. For those months she is unemployed, but nothing is wrong with the economy. She is searching for a good match, and hospitals are checking whether she fits. This is *frictional unemployment*: the time people spend moving between jobs or entering the workforce. It includes a worker who quits to find a better position and a parent returning to work after years at home.

Frictional unemployment is not all bad. A worker who takes the first offer may end up in a job that wastes her skills. Searching a few extra weeks can raise both her pay and her productivity. Job websites have made searching faster. *Unemployment insurance*, weekly payments to workers who lose a job through no fault of their own, gives a laid-off worker time to find a better fit. Economists note that the same payments can also stretch out a search, and they disagree about how large that effect is.

*Seasonal unemployment* follows the calendar. Lifeguards at Lake Michigan beaches have no work in January. Construction slows in an Illinois winter. Farm workers are busiest at planting and harvest. Stores hire extra help for the holidays and let much of it go in January. The pattern repeats every year, so by itself it says little about the health of the economy.

That is why the BLS publishes a *seasonally adjusted* unemployment rate. Suppose, in an example, the raw rate usually rises from 3.8% in December to 4.4% in January as holiday jobs end. If this January's raw rate is 4.4%, the adjusted rate shows no change, because the rise was the normal seasonal one. If the raw rate jumped to 5.0%, the extra 0.6 points would show up as real weakness. Headline numbers are almost always seasonally adjusted.

words.d: unemployment while people search for jobs, move between jobs or enter the workforce
unemployment that rises and falls with the seasons, such as winter construction or summer lifeguard work
changed to remove the normal yearly pattern so that real changes stand out
weekly payments for a limited time to workers who lose a job through no fault of their own

look.title: Why Is This Person Unemployed?
look.text: A software developer quit last month to look for a job closer to her family. A snowplow driver in Springfield has no work in June. A lifeguard at a Chicago beach is jobless every winter. A teenager just finished high school and is applying for jobs.
look.prompt: Which kind of unemployment fits each case? Does any of them signal a problem in the economy? Explain.

check.q: A new graduate spends two months searching for her first job. This is:
check.why: Time spent entering the workforce and searching for a match is frictional unemployment.

check.q: Why does the BLS seasonally adjust the unemployment rate?
choices: To remove the normal yearly pattern so real changes stand out
To leave teenagers out of the count
check.why: Rates rise and fall with the seasons every year. Adjusting removes that pattern so a real change is visible.

check.q: A ski instructor in Wisconsin is out of work every summer. This is:
check.why: The job loss follows the calendar and repeats each year, which is seasonal unemployment.

lessons.title: Mismatch and Recession
lessons.mainIdea: Structural unemployment comes from a mismatch between workers and the jobs available; cyclical unemployment comes from a weak economy.
reading: A steel mill closes and 800 workers lose their jobs. Across town, hospitals cannot fill openings for medical technicians, and software firms are hiring. There are jobs, just not jobs these workers are trained for or live near. This is *structural unemployment*: a lasting mismatch between the skills or locations of workers and the jobs available. It comes from changes in technology, in what consumers buy, and in where production happens. It can last for years, because retraining and moving take time and money.

Structural unemployment can be painful even when the overall economy is healthy. When many factories in the Midwest, including in Illinois, cut jobs in the 1980s, workers in their forties and fifties faced whole new careers. Responses include job-training programs, community college courses and help moving to where the jobs are. Economists debate how well such programs work. Some studies show solid gains in pay; others show little.

*Cyclical unemployment* is different. It rises when the whole economy slows in a *recession* and falls when it recovers. Businesses sell less, so they need fewer workers in almost every industry at once. In 2008 and 2009, home building collapsed and then the slowdown spread. Carpenters, factory workers, salespeople and office staff lost jobs whose skills were still useful. The problem was not a mismatch but too little spending in the economy overall.

Telling the two apart matters for policy. If unemployment is cyclical, the fix is a stronger economy, through more spending, lower interest rates or simply time. Those tools of fiscal and monetary policy come in later units. If it is structural, a stronger economy helps less, and training or moving matters more. A common mistake is to blame every job loss on technology, or every one on recession. The same laid-off worker can face both at once.

words.d: unemployment caused by a lasting mismatch between workers' skills or locations and the jobs available
unemployment caused by a slowdown in the whole economy; it rises in recessions and falls in recoveries
a broad decline in economic activity across the economy, lasting more than a few months

look.title: Diagnose the Job Loss
look.text: Case 1: A printing plant closes because newspapers have moved online, and its press operators find few printing jobs anywhere. Case 2: During a recession, a car dealer lays off three salespeople because fewer people are buying cars; the dealer plans to rehire when sales recover. Case 3: A bank replaces most of its tellers with apps and cash machines.
look.prompt: Label each case structural or cyclical. For each, name one policy that would help those workers most.

check.q: Coal mining jobs disappear as power plants switch to natural gas, and the miners lack skills for nearby openings. This is:
check.why: A lasting shift in the economy left the miners' skills mismatched with the jobs available. That is structural.

check.q: During a recession, unemployment rises in almost every industry at once. This rise is mainly:
check.why: Job losses across the whole economy caused by weak spending are cyclical unemployment.

check.q: Which policy fits structural unemployment best?
choices: Job training in skills employers are hiring for
Waiting for the next economic boom
check.why: Structural unemployment is a skills or location mismatch, so training fixes the cause. A boom helps cyclical unemployment more.

lessons.title: Full Employment and the Natural Rate
lessons.mainIdea: Full employment does not mean zero unemployment; it means only frictional and structural unemployment remain, at the natural rate.
reading: If unemployment could fall to zero, every graduate would start work the day after graduation. No one would ever quit to look for something better, and no factory would ever close. That is not how a changing economy works. So economists define *full employment* as the level at which there is no cyclical unemployment. Frictional and structural unemployment still remain. The unemployment rate at full employment is called the *natural rate of unemployment*.

The natural rate cannot be measured directly; it has to be estimated. Many estimates for the United States in recent years fall roughly between 4% and 5%. If the actual rate is 7% and the natural rate is 4.5%, cyclical unemployment is about 7 - 4.5 = 2.5 percentage points. If the actual rate falls well below the natural rate, say to 3%, employers compete hard for scarce workers. They raise wages, and prices can start rising faster. That is one link between jobs and inflation.

Congress has made high employment a national goal. The Employment Act of 1946 committed the federal government to promote maximum employment. A 1977 amendment to the Federal Reserve Act directs the Fed to promote maximum employment and stable prices. This pair of goals is known as the Fed's *dual mandate*. The two halves of this chapter, prices and jobs, are exactly the two things the Fed is told to watch.

The natural rate can change over time. Better job-matching websites may shorten frictional searches and lower it. A wave of factory closings may raise structural unemployment and push it up for a while. Economists disagree about how low unemployment can go before inflation speeds up. The late 2010s surprised many of them, when unemployment fell below 4% without much rise in inflation. Estimates of the natural rate are best read as ranges, not exact targets.

words.d: the level of employment at which there is no cyclical unemployment; frictional and structural unemployment remain
the unemployment rate at full employment, made up of frictional and structural unemployment
the Federal Reserve's two goals set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices

look.title: The Law Behind the Mandate
look.text: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Open Market Committee shall maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates commensurate with the economy's long run potential to increase production, so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
look.cite: Federal Reserve Act, Section 2A, as amended in 1977
look.prompt: Which two goals in this sentence match the two halves of this chapter? Why might those two goals sometimes pull against each other?

check.q: Actual unemployment is 6.5% and the natural rate is 4.5%. Cyclical unemployment is:
check.why: Cyclical = actual - natural = 6.5 - 4.5 = 2 percentage points.

check.q: Full employment means:
choices: There is no cyclical unemployment, though frictional and structural remain
check.why: Some people are always between jobs or retraining. Full employment means only that the cyclical part is gone.

check.q: The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is:
choices: Low taxes and a balanced budget
Free trade and a strong dollar
check.why: Congress directs the Fed to promote maximum employment and stable prices. The Fed treats 2% inflation, not zero, as stable.

review.q: A market basket costs $400 in the base year and $436 this year. The price index this year is:
review.why: Index = 436 / 400 x 100 = 109. Prices are 9% above the base year.

review.q: The CPI rises from 280 to 294. The inflation rate is:
Carlos earned $20 an hour last year and $21 this year, while prices rose 8%. His real wage:
review.why: His raise was 1 / 20 = 5%. Real wage growth is about 5 - 8 = -3%, so his pay buys less.

review.q: Which person gains from unexpectedly high inflation?
choices: A retiree on a fixed pension
A saver with cash in a jar
A homeowner with a fixed-rate mortgage
review.why: The homeowner repays a fixed number of dollars that are now worth less. The others hold or receive fixed dollars.

review.q: A county has 90,000 employed, 10,000 unemployed and 60,000 adults not in the labor force. The unemployment rate is:
review.why: Labor force = 100,000. Rate = 10,000 / 100,000 x 100 = 10%. Dividing by all 160,000 adults gives the wrong 6.25%.

review.q: A county has 160,000 adults. Of them, 90,000 are employed and 10,000 are unemployed. The labor force participation rate is:
A factory worker loses her job when her plant is automated, and nearby openings need computer skills she lacks. This is:
review.why: A lasting change in technology left her skills mismatched with the jobs available, which is structural unemployment.

review.q: The unemployment rate falls because thousands of discouraged workers stop looking for jobs. What else would you expect to see?
choices: A rise in the participation rate
A rise in the number employed
A fall in the labor force participation rate
review.why: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so participation falls. No one was hired, so employment does not rise.
